title: Python Scripting and Linux for DevOps
subtitle: Automate Linux servers with Python: scripts that manage files and run commands safely, command-line tools built with argparse and click, packages installed by script, and jobs scheduled with cron and systemd.
skills: Log analysis with grep, awk and sed
outcomes: Write Python scripts that manage files, update configuration safely and run Linux commands with subprocess, failing with clear messages and exit statuses
Build command-line tools with argparse and click, with subcommands, help text, validated input and tests
Investigate a server with grep, awk, sed, find and the monitoring tools, and write Python filters that work in pipelines
Manage packages with apt and dnf, and automate installs so a script can be run again safely
Schedule and supervise Python automation with cron and systemd timers, configured by environment variables and recorded with logging
prerequisites: Linux Command Line Essentials, or the same comfort in a Linux shell (files, permissions, pipes and simple scripts), and basic Python: variables, functions, loops, lists and dictionaries, as in Python Programming with PyCharm. You need a Linux machine where you can use sudo, such as Ubuntu 24.04 on WSL, in a virtual machine or on a cloud server, with Python 3.11 or later and python3-venv. Docker is optional, for trying installs in a throwaway container.
description:
DevOps work is full of small jobs that come round again and again: tidy the logs, check the disks, install the same packages on every new server, find out what went wrong at 09:14. This course teaches you to automate them with Python on Linux, building on the shell skills from Linux Command Line Essentials. You'll write scripts that manage files and configuration safely and run commands with subprocess; turn them into proper command-line tools with argparse and click, with help, validation and tests; investigate a disk-space incident with grep, awk, sed, find and the monitoring tools, adding your own Python filters to the pipeline; script package installs with apt and dnf so they can be run again safely; and leave your automation running with cron and systemd timers, configured by environment variables and recorded with logging.

Every module ends with a hands-on lab on files that come with the course, with the exact output a correct solution prints, and the course ends with devsetup, a click tool you build to set up a developer machine from a profile: packages, folders and configuration files, safely and repeatably.

modules.title: Python Scripting for SysAdmins
modules.summary: Use Python for the jobs that outgrow a shell script: files and directories with pathlib and shutil, configuration files read and written safely, Linux commands run with subprocess, and errors reported with clear messages and exit statuses.

lessons.title: From shell scripts to Python scripts
objectives: Decide when a task has outgrown a shell script and belongs in Python
Write a Python script that runs like any Linux command, with a shebang, arguments and an exit status
key_points: Bash is good at gluing a few commands together. Move to Python when a task needs data structures, parsing JSON or CSV, careful error handling, tests, or the same behaviour on several systems.

A script runs like a command when its first line is #!/usr/bin/env python3 and it's executable (chmod +x tool.py). Putting the work in main() under if __name__ == "__main__": stops it running when another module imports the file.

sys.argv is the list of command-line arguments, with the script's own name first. sys.stdin, sys.stdout and sys.stderr are the three standard streams: print(message, file=sys.stderr) writes an error message.

sys.exit(0) ends with success and any other number means failure; sys.exit("message") prints the message to standard error and exits with status 1. Shells, cron, systemd and CI pipelines all judge a script by this status.

On Ubuntu 23.04 and later and on Debian 12, pip refuses to install into the system Python (externally-managed-environment). Give each tool a virtual environment: python3 -m venv .venv, from the python3-venv package.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Print a one-line summary of this machine."""
import os
import platform
import sys


def main() -> int:
    if len(sys.argv) > 1:
        print(f"usage: {sys.argv[0]}  (takes no arguments)", file=sys.stderr)
        return 2

    print(f"{platform.node()} {platform.system()} {platform.release()} "
          f"cpus={os.cpu_count()} load={load1:.2f}")
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

lessons.title: Files and directories with pathlib, os and shutil
objectives: Inspect, create and find files and directories with pathlib
Copy, move and delete files safely with shutil
Build paths that work wherever a script is started from
key_points: pathlib.Path treats a path as an object: Path("/var/log") / "nginx" / "access.log" joins the parts, and .name, .stem, .suffix and .parent take a path apart, so there's no fragile string joining.

Path methods do the everyday jobs: .exists(), .is_file(), .is_dir(), .mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True), which is safe to run twice, .glob("*.log") in one directory and .rglob("*.log") through a whole tree.
.stat() gives a file's size in bytes (st_size) and its last modification time (st_mtime, in seconds since 1970); compare st_mtime with time.time() to find files older than a number of days.
shutil.copy2 copies a file with its timestamps and permissions, shutil.copytree copies a directory, shutil.move moves across file systems, and shutil.rmtree deletes a whole tree, with no undo.
Prefer Python's own functions to parsing command output: shutil.disk_usage("/") gives total, used and free bytes, and shutil.which("nginx") gives a program's path on PATH, or None.

Relative paths are resolved against the current working directory, which is your home directory under cron and / for a systemd system service. Build paths from absolute ones or from Path(__file__).resolve().parent.

lessons.title: Reading and updating configuration files
objectives: Read and update INI, JSON and TOML configuration from Python
Write configuration files atomically and idempotently, so a crash or a second run does no harm
key_points: Open text files in a with block with an explicit encoding: open(path, encoding="utf-8"). Mode "w" empties the file first, "a" appends, and "x" creates a new file but fails if one already exists.

configparser reads INI files: config["server"]["port"] is always a string, so use getint(), getfloat() or getboolean() to convert it, with fallback= for a default. It doesn't keep comments when it writes a file back.

json.load and json.dump(data, f, indent=2) read and write JSON. tomllib (Python 3.11+) reads TOML from a file opened in binary mode ("rb") but can't write it. For YAML, use PyYAML's yaml.safe_load, never yaml.load, on files you didn't write.
Write configuration atomically: write the new content to a temporary file in the same directory, then os.replace() it over the old one, so readers see the old file or the new one, never half of each.
tempfile.mkstemp creates its file with 600 permissions, so copy the original's mode with shutil.copymode before the replace, or a world-readable config quietly becomes private.
Make changes idempotent: compare the new content with what's there and write only when it differs, so running the script twice changes nothing the second time, and says so.

steps.do: Create set_option.py: it changes one option, writes the file atomically, and skips the write when nothing would change.
steps.code:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Set one option in an INI file, safely: ./set_option.py FILE SECTION OPTION VALUE"""
import configparser
import io
import os
import shutil
import sys
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path


def write_atomic(path: Path, text: str) -> None:
    """Write text to a temporary file next to path, then rename it over path in one step."""
    fd, tmp = tempfile.mkstemp(dir=path.parent, prefix=f".{path.name}.")
    with os.fdopen(fd, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write(text)
    shutil.copymode(path, tmp)  # mkstemp makes the file 600; keep the original's permissions
    os.replace(tmp, path)


def main() -> int:
    if len(sys.argv) != 5:
        print(f"usage: {sys.argv[0]} FILE SECTION OPTION VALUE", file=sys.stderr)
        return 2
    path, section, option, value = Path(sys.argv[1]), *sys.argv[2:]
    config = configparser.ConfigParser()
    config.read(path, encoding="utf-8")
    if config.get(section, option, fallback=None) == value:
        print(f"no change: {section}.{option} is already {value}")
        return 0
    if not config.has_section(section):
        config.add_section(section)
    config[section][option] = value
    buffer = io.StringIO()
    config.write(buffer)
    write_atomic(path, buffer.getvalue())
    print(f"updated {path}: {section}.{option} = {value}")
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

lessons.title: Running commands with subprocess, and handling errors
objectives: Run Linux commands from Python and use their output and exit status
Handle the errors automation meets with try and except, and report them clearly
key_points: subprocess.run(["df", "-h", "/"], capture_output=True, text=True) runs a command and returns a CompletedProcess with returncode, stdout and stderr; text=True gives strings instead of bytes.

Pass the command as a list of arguments. A string with shell=True goes through a shell, so a file name containing spaces or ; can break the command or run another one; shlex.split() turns a command line into a safe list.
check=True raises CalledProcessError when the command exits non-zero, timeout=30 raises TimeoutExpired if it hangs, and a program that isn't installed raises FileNotFoundError.

Catch the specific exceptions you can handle, such as FileNotFoundError, PermissionError or CalledProcessError; use else for code that runs only on success and finally for clean-up. A bare except: hides real bugs.
A good automation script says what failed on standard error and exits non-zero, so cron, systemd and pipelines see the failure instead of a traceback or a silent success.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Create a sample log folder for the housekeeping lab: python3 make_sample.py

It (re)creates sample/var/log/shop/ with log files of known sizes and ages, so you can
run the lab as often as you like and always start from the same state.
"""
import os
import shutil
import time
from pathlib import Path

LOG_DIR = Path("sample/var/log/shop")
DAY = 24 * 60 * 60

# file name: (age in days, size in KiB)
FILES = {
    "app.log": (0, 12),
    "app.log.1": (2, 10),
    "app.log.2": (9, 8),
    "app.log.3": (16, 8),
    "worker.log": (0, 6),
    "worker.log.1": (12, 4),
    "notes.txt": (30, 1),
}


def main() -> None:
    shutil.rmtree("sample", ignore_errors=True)
    LOG_DIR.mkdir(parents=True)
    now = time.time()
    for name, (age_days, size_kib) in FILES.items():
        path = LOG_DIR / name
        line = f"2025-06-01T08:00:00Z INFO {name} sample line\n"
        size = size_kib * 1024
        path.write_text((line * (size // len(line) + 1))[:size], encoding="utf-8")
        mtime = now - age_days * DAY - 60  # a minute in the past
        os.utime(path, (mtime, mtime))
    print(f"Created {len(FILES)} files in {LOG_DIR}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

[housekeeping]
# Paths are relative to this file's folder (or absolute).
log_dir = sample/var/log/shop
archive_dir = sample/archive
# Rotated logs are named like app.log.1, app.log.2 ...
pattern = *.log.*
# Archive rotated logs older than this many days.
max_age_days = 7

[housekeeping]
log_dir = sample/var/log/missing
archive_dir = sample/archive
pattern = *.log.*
max_age_days = 7

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Archive old rotated logs: compress each into an archive folder, test it, then remove the original.

Usage: ./housekeeping.py CONFIG_FILE
"""
import configparser
import gzip
import os
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys
import time
from pathlib import Path

DAY = 24 * 60 * 60


def show(path: Path) -> str:
    """A path as messages show it: relative to the current directory."""
    return os.path.relpath(path)


def load_config(path: Path) -> dict:
    """Read the [housekeeping] section. Paths in it are relative to the config file's folder."""
    if not path.is_file():
        raise FileNotFoundError(f"config file not found: {path}")
    parser = configparser.ConfigParser()
    parser.read(path, encoding="utf-8")
    section = parser["housekeeping"]
    base = path.resolve().parent
    # TODO 1: read max_age_days as a whole number with section.getint(), with a fallback of 7
    max_age_days = 7
    return {
        "log_dir": base / section["log_dir"],
        "archive_dir": base / section["archive_dir"],
        "pattern": section.get("pattern", "*.log.*"),
        "max_age_days": max_age_days,
    }


def find_old_logs(log_dir: Path, pattern: str, max_age_days: int) -> list[Path]:
    """The files in log_dir that match pattern and are older than max_age_days, oldest first."""
    cutoff = time.time() - max_age_days * DAY
    # TODO 2: list the files in log_dir.glob(pattern) whose .stat().st_mtime is older than cutoff
    #         (skip anything that isn't a file), and return them sorted by st_mtime, oldest first
    old = []
    return old


def archive(path: Path, archive_dir: Path) -> Path:
    """Compress path into archive_dir as NAME.gz, test the archive with gzip -t, then delete the original."""
    archive_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    target = archive_dir / (path.name + ".gz")
    with path.open("rb") as src, gzip.open(target, "wb") as dst:
        shutil.copyfileobj(src, dst)
    # TODO 3: test the archive with the command  gzip -t TARGET  using subprocess.run: pass the command as a
    #         list, with check=True, capture_output=True, text=True and timeout=60. Then delete the original.
    return target


def main() -> int:
    if len(sys.argv) != 2:
        print(f"usage: {sys.argv[0]} CONFIG_FILE", file=sys.stderr)
        return 2
    # TODO 4: put the next line in a try block. On FileNotFoundError, print "error: " and the exception to
    #         standard error and return 2; on KeyError or ValueError, print "error: bad config: " and the
    #         exception to standard error and return 2.
    cfg = load_config(Path(sys.argv[1]))

    log_dir = cfg["log_dir"]
    if not log_dir.is_dir():
        print(f"error: log directory does not exist: {show(log_dir)}", file=sys.stderr)
        return 1

    old = find_old_logs(log_dir, cfg["pattern"], cfg["max_age_days"])
    print(f"Found {len(old)} log(s) older than {cfg['max_age_days']} days in {show(log_dir)}")
    total = 0
    for path in old:
        size = path.stat().st_size
        try:
            target = archive(path, cfg["archive_dir"])
        except (OSError, subprocess.SubprocessError) as e:
            print(f"error: could not archive {path.name}: {e}", file=sys.stderr)
            return 1
        total += size
        print(f"archived {path.name} -> {show(target)}")
    if old:
        print(f"Archived {len(old)} file(s), {total:,} bytes before compression")
    else:
        print("Nothing to archive")
    usage = shutil.disk_usage(log_dir)
    print(f"Disk free: {usage.free / usage.total:.0%}")
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

hints: If every run finds 0 logs, check TODO 2: a file is old when its st_mtime is less than (earlier than) the cutoff.
sorted(old, key=lambda p: p.stat().st_mtime) puts the oldest file first.
If gzip -t fails, print e.stderr from the CalledProcessError to see why.
Run python3 make_sample.py at any time to start again with fresh sample files.

modules.title: Building Robust CLI Tools
modules.summary: Turn scripts into tools other people can rely on: arguments, options and subcommands with argparse and click, help that explains itself, validation that rejects bad input before anything changes, tests with CliRunner, and installing the tool as a command.

lessons.title: Command-line interfaces with argparse
objectives: Define positional arguments, options and flags with argparse
Let types, choices and defaults validate input for you
Organise a bigger tool into subcommands
key_points: argparse, in the standard library, turns sys.argv into named values: add_argument("paths", nargs="+") adds a required positional argument taking one or more values, and add_argument("--warn", type=int, default=90) an optional one.

type= converts and checks a value (type=int rejects "abc"), choices= limits it to a list, action="store_true" makes a flag such as --dry-run, and metavar= and help= control how it appears in the help.
argparse writes -h/--help from your help= texts; on bad input it prints the usage line and an error to standard error and exits with status 2, the usual status for wrong usage.
Check what types can't, such as a range or a combination of options, after parsing, and report it with parser.error("..."), which prints the usage and exits with status 2, like argparse's own errors.
Subcommands, like git commit and git push, come from parser.add_subparsers(dest="command", required=True); each subparser gets its own arguments, and set_defaults(func=...) picks the function to run.

lessons.title: Building tools with click
objectives: Build a click command with options, arguments and subcommands
Validate input with click's parameter types and report errors cleanly
key_points: click builds a command-line interface from decorators: @click.command() makes a function a command, and @click.option("--days", default=7, show_default=True) and @click.argument("directory") declare inputs that arrive as the function's arguments.
Parameter types validate before your code runs: click.IntRange(1, 365), click.Choice(["text", "json"]) and click.Path(exists=True, file_okay=False, path_type=Path) for a directory that must exist.
is_flag=True makes an on/off option, envvar="LOGTOOL_DIR" lets an environment variable supply a value, and prompt=True with hide_input=True asks for a secret without showing it.
@click.group() makes a command with subcommands: each function decorated with @cli.command() becomes one, as in logs old and logs size, and --help lists them all.
click.echo() prints, with err=True for standard error. Raising click.ClickException("message") prints Error: message and exits with status 1; bad usage exits with status 2.
click is a third-party package (pip install click), while argparse needs nothing installed, so argparse suits small scripts that must run on any machine with Python.

Test a click command with CliRunner
Package a tool so pip installs it as a command
key_points: Good help says what the tool does and shows an example, and every option has a one-line help text and a visible default; in click, the function's docstring becomes the command's help.

click.testing.CliRunner runs a command in-process: result = CliRunner().invoke(cli, ["slow", "app.log", "--limit", "3"]) gives result.exit_code, result.output and, from click 8.2, result.stdout and result.stderr separately.

A pyproject.toml with [project.scripts] logtool = "logtool.cli:cli" makes pip install create a logtool command; pip install -e . (editable) runs your source folder, so changes apply without reinstalling.
pipx installs each command-line tool into its own virtual environment and puts the command on your PATH, so tools never clash with each other or with the system's Python (sudo apt install pipx).

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Write two days of sample application logs to logs/: python3 make_logs.py

The logs are the same every time (a fixed random seed), so your answers can be checked.
Each line looks like this:
2025-06-01T08:00:31Z INFO orders method=GET path=/api/orders status=200 duration_ms=87 user=ana@example.com
"""
import random
from pathlib import Path

SERVICES = ["orders", "payments", "catalog", "auth"]
PATHS = {"orders": "/api/orders", "payments": "/api/payments", "catalog": "/api/products", "auth": "/api/login"}
USERS = ["ana", "bilal", "chen", "dara", "emeka", "farah"]


def pick(rng: random.Random, items: list):
    return items[int(rng.random() * len(items))]


def make_day(day: str, seed: int, count: int) -> list[str]:
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    lines = []
    seconds = 8 * 3600  # the first line is just after 08:00
    for _ in range(count):
        seconds += 5 + int(rng.random() * 40)
        hh, mm, ss = seconds // 3600, seconds // 60 % 60, seconds % 60
        service = pick(rng, SERVICES)
        method = "POST" if service != "catalog" and rng.random() < 0.4 else "GET"
        duration = 20 + int(rng.random() * 180)
        status, level = 200, "INFO"
        roll = rng.random()
        if roll < 0.06:
            status, level = pick(rng, [500, 503]), "ERROR"
        elif roll < 0.14:
            duration, level = 900 + int(rng.random() * 2100), "WARNING"
        elif roll < 0.20:
            status = pick(rng, [400, 401, 404])
        user = pick(rng, USERS)
        lines.append(f"{day}T{hh:02d}:{mm:02d}:{ss:02d}Z {level} {service} method={method} "
                     f"path={PATHS[service]} status={status} duration_ms={duration} user={user}@example.com")
    return lines


def main() -> None:
    out = Path("logs")
    out.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    for day, seed in [("2025-06-01", 1), ("2025-06-02", 2)]:
        path = out / f"shop-{day}.log"
        path.write_text("\n".join(make_day(day, seed, 150)) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
        print(f"wrote {path}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""logtool: answer common questions about the shop's application logs."""

import json

from click.testing import CliRunner

from logtool.cli import cli

LINES = [
    "2025-06-01T08:00:05Z INFO orders method=GET path=/api/orders status=200 duration_ms=40 user=ana@example.com",
    "2025-06-01T08:00:09Z ERROR payments method=POST path=/api/payments status=503 duration_ms=120 user=chen@example.com",
    "2025-06-01T08:00:15Z WARNING catalog method=GET path=/api/products status=200 duration_ms=1500 user=dara@example.com",
    "2025-06-01T08:00:20Z ERROR orders method=POST path=/api/orders status=500 duration_ms=80 user=ana@example.com",
]


def make_log(tmp_path):
    path = tmp_path / "shop.log"
    path.write_text("\n".join(LINES) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
    return str(path)


def test_levels_counts_each_level(tmp_path):
    result = CliRunner().invoke(cli, ["levels", make_log(tmp_path)])
    assert result.exit_code == 0
    assert result.output.splitlines() == ["ERROR       2", "WARNING     1", "INFO        1"]


def test_slow_lists_only_requests_over_the_limit(tmp_path):
    result = CliRunner().invoke(cli, ["slow", make_log(tmp_path), "--min-ms", "100"])
    assert result.exit_code == 0
    assert result.stdout.splitlines()[0].startswith(" 1500 ms")
    assert "2 request(s) took 100 ms or more" in result.stderr


def test_errors_can_filter_by_service(tmp_path):
    result = CliRunner().invoke(cli, ["errors", make_log(tmp_path), "--service", "payments"])
    assert result.exit_code == 0
    assert "503" in result.stdout
    assert "orders" not in result.stdout


def test_a_missing_file_is_a_usage_error(tmp_path):
    result = CliRunner().invoke(cli, ["levels", str(tmp_path / "nope.log")])
    assert result.exit_code == 2
    assert "does not exist" in result.output


# TODO 3: add two tests:

modules.title: Core Linux Utilities
modules.summary: The utilities DevOps engineers reach for every day, used for operations work: searching and reshaping logs with grep, awk and sed, finding files with find, xargs and locate, reading a system's health with top, htop and friends, and Python filters that fit into pipelines. It builds on the basics in Linux Command Line Essentials.

lessons.title: grep, awk and sed for operations work
objectives: Search many logs at once, including rotated and compressed ones, with grep's recursive and context options
Summarise and rewrite log lines with awk and sed
key_points: grep -r searches a whole directory tree, -l lists only the names of matching files, -o prints only the matching part of each line, and -A 2, -B 2 or -C 2 add lines after, before or around each match, such as the lines leading up to an error.

grep -F treats the pattern as fixed text, so dots and brackets aren't special; -w matches whole words only; -m 1 stops at the first match; and zgrep searches gzip-compressed rotated logs, and plain ones, without unpacking them.

awk's associative arrays total by key in one pass: awk '{n[$3]++} END {for (s in n) print s, n[s]}' counts the lines for each value of the third field, and printf "%-10s %5d\n" prints aligned columns.
For key=value fields, split() pulls out the value: awk '{split($7, d, "="); total += d[2]} END {print total / NR}' averages the duration_ms field over all lines.
sed -E 's/user=[^@ ]+@/user=***@/' rewrites part of every line with an extended regular expression, and sed -n '/T08:10:/,/T08:12:/p' prints the lines from one match to the next.
When a pipeline grows past a few stages, or needs dates, JSON or error handling, move it into a Python script, which is easier to read, test and change.

lessons.title: Finding files: find, xargs and locate
objectives: Find files by name, type, size, age and permissions with find
Act on many files safely with -exec, -delete and xargs
Choose between find and locate
key_points: find combines tests: find /var/log -type f -name '*.gz' -mtime +30 finds compressed logs last changed more than 30 days ago; -size +100M finds big files, -perm -o+w world-writable ones, -newer ref files changed after ref, and -maxdepth 1 stops it descending.

-mtime counts whole days and drops the fraction, so -mtime +7 matches files at least eight days old and -mtime -1 files changed in the last 24 hours; -mmin works in minutes. -size rounds up to whole units, so -size +8k skips a file of exactly 8 KiB.

-exec cmd {} + runs the command once with many file names, -exec cmd {} \; once per file, and -delete removes what was found. Run the same find without the action first, to see exactly what it will touch.
find ... -print0 | xargs -0 cmd separates names with null characters, so names containing spaces, or even newlines, are handled safely; xargs -P 4 runs four commands at a time.

locate (plocate on recent Ubuntu) searches a prebuilt index of file names, so it's much faster than find, but it only knows what existed when updatedb last ran, usually once a day, and it can't test sizes or dates.

lessons.title: Watching the system: top, htop and the monitoring toolkit
objectives: Read load, CPU, memory and disk figures from top, htop, free, df and du
Collect the same figures in scripts with batch modes and /proc
key_points: top shows processes live, busiest first. Its header has the load averages, task counts, CPU time split into us (user), sy (system), id (idle) and wa (waiting for I/O), and memory; P sorts by CPU, M by memory and q quits. htop adds colour, scrolling and a tree view (F5).

The load average is the average number of processes running or waiting to run over the last 1, 5 and 15 minutes; on Linux it also counts processes waiting for disk I/O. Compare it with the number of CPU cores, from nproc.
free -h shows memory. Read the available column, not free: Linux uses spare memory as a disk cache and gives it back when programs need it, so low free memory on its own isn't a problem.
df -h shows the space on each file system and df -i its inodes (file slots), because a disk can fill up with many small files; du -sh /var/log/* | sort -h shows what's using the space.

Deleting a log file that a running program still has open doesn't free its space until the program closes it. Empty it with truncate -s 0 instead, or restart the program; lsof +L1 lists deleted files that are still open.

For scripts, use the non-interactive forms: top -b -n 1 prints one snapshot, ps -eo pid,user,%cpu,%mem,comm --sort=-%cpu lists the busiest processes, and /proc/loadavg and /proc/meminfo hold the raw numbers.

lessons.title: Pipes, redirection and Python in the pipeline
objectives: Write Python filters that read standard input and write standard output, so they slot into pipelines
Use redirection and exit statuses correctly when Python and shell tools work together
key_points: A Python filter reads lines from sys.stdin and prints its results, so it works anywhere in a pipeline: grep ' payments ' app.log | python3 durations.py | tee summary.txt.
Put data on standard output and messages on standard error. Then > and | carry only the data and the user still sees the warnings, while 2> errors.txt or 2>&1 decides where the messages go.
fileinput.input() reads the files named on the command line or, when there are none, standard input, the way grep, sort and awk behave.
When output is piped into head, the reader may close the pipe early and Python raises BrokenPipeError; a well-behaved filter catches it and exits quietly instead of printing a traceback.

A pipeline's exit status is its last command's; set -o pipefail in Bash makes any failing stage fail the whole pipeline. From Python, subprocess.run(cmd, input=text, capture_output=True, text=True) feeds a command without a shell.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Build the incident/ folder for the module 3 lab: python3 make_incident.py

It recreates a small copy of a server's disk the morning a disk-space alert fired:
logs (current, rotated and compressed), temporary uploads and old release archives.
Everything is the same every time you run it, except that file ages count back from now.
"""
import gzip
import io
import os
import random
import shutil
import tarfile
import time
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path("incident")
DAY = 24 * 60 * 60
SERVICES = ["orders", "payments", "catalog", "auth"]
PATHS = {"orders": "/api/orders", "payments": "/api/payments", "catalog": "/api/products", "auth": "/api/login"}
USERS = ["ana", "bilal", "chen", "dara", "emeka", "farah"]


def pick(rng, items):
    return items[int(rng.random() * len(items))]


def log_lines(day: str, seed: int, count: int, burst: bool = False) -> list[str]:
    """count log lines from 08:00. With burst, payments fails from 09:12 to 09:16, orders with it,
    and every failed payment is retried twice."""
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    lines = []
    seconds = 8 * 3600
    for _ in range(count):
        in_burst = burst and 9 * 3600 + 12 * 60 <= seconds < 9 * 3600 + 16 * 60
        seconds += (3 + int(rng.random() * 6)) if in_burst else (5 + int(rng.random() * 30))
        hh, mm, ss = seconds // 3600, seconds // 60 % 60, seconds % 60
        service = pick(rng, SERVICES)
        method = "POST" if service != "catalog" and rng.random() < 0.4 else "GET"
        duration = 20 + int(rng.random() * 180)
        status, level = 200, "INFO"
        roll = rng.random()
        if in_burst and service in ("payments", "orders"):
            status, level, duration = 503, "ERROR", 3000 + int(rng.random() * 2000)
        elif roll < 0.04:
            status, level = pick(rng, [500, 503]), "ERROR"
        elif roll < 0.10:
            duration, level = 900 + int(rng.random() * 2100), "WARNING"
        user = pick(rng, USERS)
        lines.append(f"{day}T{hh:02d}:{mm:02d}:{ss:02d}Z {level} {service} method={method} "
                     f"path={PATHS[service]} status={status} duration_ms={duration} user={user}@example.com")
        if in_burst and service == "payments":
            for retry in (1, 2):
                lines.append(f"{day}T{hh:02d}:{mm:02d}:{ss:02d}Z ERROR payments method=POST path=/api/payments "
                             f"status=503 duration_ms=3000 user={user}@example.com retry={retry}")
    return lines


def write(path: Path, data: bytes, age_days: float) -> None:
    path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    path.write_bytes(data)
    mtime = time.time() - age_days * DAY
    os.utime(path, (mtime, mtime))


def tar_bytes(name: str, size: int) -> bytes:
    """A real (uncompressed) tar archive holding one file of the given size."""
    buffer = io.BytesIO()
    with tarfile.open(fileobj=buffer, mode="w", format=tarfile.USTAR_FORMAT) as tar:
        info = tarfile.TarInfo(f"{name}/app.bin")
        info.size, info.mtime = size, 1717200000
        tar.addfile(info, io.BytesIO(bytes(range(256)) * (size // 256)))
    return buffer.getvalue()


def main() -> None:
    shutil.rmtree(ROOT, ignore_errors=True)
    logs = ROOT / "var/log/shop"
    text = lambda lines: ("\n".join(lines) + "\n").encode()
    write(logs / "shop.log", text(log_lines("2025-06-03", 3, 260, burst=True)), 0.01)
    write(logs / "shop.log.1", text(log_lines("2025-06-02", 2, 200)), 1)
    for n, (day, seed) in enumerate([("2025-06-01", 1), ("2025-05-31", 31), ("2025-05-30", 30)], start=2):
        write(logs / f"shop.log.{n}.gz", gzip.compress(text(log_lines(day, seed, 200)), mtime=0), n)
    debug = "".join(f"2025-06-03T09:{i // 4000 % 60:02d}:00Z DEBUG payments cache lookup key=basket:{i:07d} hit=false\n"
                    for i in range(80000))
    write(logs / "debug-trace.log", debug.encode(), 0.01)
    for i, age in enumerate([40, 35, 30, 21, 3]):
        write(ROOT / f"var/tmp/upload-{i + 1}.tmp", bytes(300 * 1024), age)
    write(ROOT / "var/tmp/report final.tmp", bytes(100 * 1024), 25)
    for version, age in [("1.4.0", 60), ("1.5.0", 45), ("1.6.0", 20), ("1.7.0", 1)]:
        write(ROOT / f"home/deploy/releases/shop-{version}.tar", tar_bytes(f"shop-{version}", 2 * 1024 * 1024), age)
    count = sum(1 for p in ROOT.rglob("*") if p.is_file())
    print(f"Created {count} files in {ROOT}/")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Count ERROR lines per minute, busiest minutes first.

Reads the log files you name, or standard input if you name none, so it works in a pipeline:
  grep -h ' ERROR ' shop.log | ./errors_per_minute.py --top 3
  zcat shop.log.*.gz | ./errors_per_minute.py
"""
import argparse
import fileinput
import os
import sys
from collections import Counter


def main() -> int:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Count ERROR lines per minute, busiest first.")
    parser.add_argument("files", nargs="*", help="log files to read (default: standard input)")
    parser.add_argument("--top", type=int, default=5, help="how many minutes to show (default: %(default)s)")
    args = parser.parse_args()

    counts: Counter[str] = Counter()
    skipped = 0
    for line in fileinput.input(args.files, encoding="utf-8"):
        # TODO: split the line into fields. If there are fewer than 3, add 1 to skipped and move on.
        #       If the second field is ERROR, add 1 to counts for the line's minute: the first
        #       16 characters of the first field, such as 2025-06-03T09:14.
        pass
    for minute, n in counts.most_common(args.top):
        print(f"{minute}  {n:>3}")
    if skipped:
        print(f"skipped {skipped} line(s) that weren't log lines", file=sys.stderr)
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":

    except BrokenPipeError:

modules.summary: How Linux package managers install software, resolve dependencies and decide which repositories to trust; apt and dnf side by side; and provisioning by script, so every fresh server gets the right packages the same way. It goes beyond the apt basics in Linux Command Line Essentials.

lessons.title: Packages, dependencies and repositories
objectives: Explain what a package manager does, from repositories and signatures to dependency resolution
Find out where a package comes from, what it depends on and which files it installed
key_points: A package bundles a program's files with metadata: its name, version, dependencies and scripts to run on install. Debian and Ubuntu use .deb packages; Red Hat Enterprise Linux, Fedora, Rocky Linux and AlmaLinux use .rpm.

Low-level tools install single package files and query what's installed (dpkg for .deb, rpm for .rpm); high-level managers, apt and dnf, download from repositories and resolve dependencies, installing whatever else a package needs.

A repository is a server holding packages and a signed index of them. apt reads its sources from /etc/apt/sources.list.d/ (Ubuntu 24.04 uses ubuntu.sources, in the deb822 format) and dnf from /etc/yum.repos.d/*.repo.

Repositories sign their indexes, and the package manager rejects data that doesn't match a trusted key. Add a third-party repository with its key in /etc/apt/keyrings and a signed-by option; apt-key is deprecated.

Look before you install: apt-cache policy nginx (dnf info nginx) shows the installed and candidate versions and their repositories, apt-cache depends nginx (dnf repoquery --requires nginx) the dependencies, and dpkg -L or rpm -ql a package's files.

lessons.title: apt and dnf side by side
objectives: Carry out everyday package tasks with apt and with dnf
Choose package commands that are safe to use in scripts
key_points: The same jobs, two tools: sudo apt update or sudo dnf check-update refreshes the package lists (dnf also refreshes when its cached copy expires), apt install or dnf install adds packages, apt remove or dnf remove uninstalls, and apt upgrade or dnf upgrade applies updates.
On RHEL 8 and later, Fedora and rebuilds such as Rocky Linux and AlmaLinux, yum is an alias for dnf, so older yum commands and scripts still work.

In scripts, use apt-get and apt-cache rather than apt, whose output may change between versions (it warns about this when its output isn't a terminal). Add -y to answer yes, and run apt-get update before installing on a fresh machine.

Set DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive so no configuration prompt waits for an answer. sudo resets the environment, so pass it with sudo env DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive apt-get install -y ..., or run as root.

Ask the package database rather than parsing friendly output: dpkg-query -W -f='${Status}' curl prints install ok installed for an installed package, and rpm -q curl exits with status 0 only when it's installed.

Pin what you depend on: apt-get install nginx=VERSION installs an exact version, apt-mark hold nginx stops upgrades changing it (apt-mark unhold releases it), and dnf's versionlock plugin does the same on Red Hat-family systems.

lessons.title: Automating installs: idempotent provisioning
objectives: Write a provisioning script that installs only what's missing and is safe to run again
Detect the distribution to choose the right package manager
Install Python tools without breaking the system Python
key_points: Provisioning takes a fresh machine to a known state by script. An idempotent script checks the current state first and changes only what differs, so running it twice is safe and the second run has nothing to do.
Check, then act: query each package, install all the missing ones in a single apt-get install call, then check again and report what changed, failing loudly if anything is still missing.

/etc/os-release identifies the distribution: ID (such as ubuntu or rocky) and ID_LIKE (debian; rhel centos fedora) tell a script whether to use apt-get or dnf. Python's platform.freedesktop_os_release() reads the file for you.

Python tools belong in virtual environments: pip inside a venv for a project's libraries, pipx for command-line tools, and system Python packages (python3-requests and the like) only through apt or dnf. Pin versions in requirements.txt.

Configuration management tools such as Ansible apply the same check-then-act idea across many machines; a script like this is enough for one machine, and for container images the Dockerfile's RUN lines do the installing.
Keep systems patched without waiting for you: unattended-upgrades installs security updates on Debian and Ubuntu, and dnf-automatic does the same on Red Hat-family systems.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Install the packages a machine needs, and only the ones that are missing.

  ./provision.py detect [--os-release FILE]      which distribution and package manager
  ./provision.py check PACKAGES_FILE             what's installed and what's missing
  ./provision.py apply PACKAGES_FILE [--dry-run] install what's missing (safe to run again)
"""
import argparse
import os
import shlex
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path


def read_os_release(path: Path) -> dict[str, str]:
    """Parse an os-release file: KEY=value lines, with the value optionally in quotes."""
    info = {}
    for line in path.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines():
        line = line.strip()
        if line and not line.startswith("#") and "=" in line:
            key, value = line.split("=", 1)
            info[key] = value.strip("\"'")
    return info


def package_manager(info: dict[str, str]) -> str:
    """apt for the Debian family (Debian, Ubuntu...), dnf for the Red Hat family (RHEL, Fedora, Rocky...)."""
    family = {info.get("ID", "")} | set(info.get("ID_LIKE", "").split())
    # TODO 1: return "apt" if family includes debian or ubuntu, and "dnf" if it includes rhel, fedora
    #         or centos (sets have & for intersection). Otherwise fall through to the error below.
    raise ValueError(f"unsupported distribution: {info.get('PRETTY_NAME', info.get('ID', 'unknown'))}")


def read_packages(path: Path) -> list[str]:
    """One package name per line; blank lines and # comments are ignored."""
    names = []
    for line in path.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines():
        name = line.split("#", 1)[0].strip()
        if name:
            names.append(name)
    return names


def is_installed(package: str, manager: str) -> bool:
    """Ask the package database, not the human-readable output of apt or dnf."""
    if manager == "apt":
        # TODO 2: run  dpkg-query -W -f=${Status} PACKAGE  (as a list, capturing text output, timeout=30)
        #         and return True only if it exits with 0 and prints exactly: install ok installed
        return False
    result = subprocess.run(["rpm", "-q", package], capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=30)
    return result.returncode == 0


def as_root(cmd: list[str]) -> list[str]:
    """Run with sudo unless we're root already (as in a container)."""
    return cmd if os.geteuid() == 0 else ["sudo", *cmd]


def install_commands(missing: list[str], manager: str) -> list[list[str]]:
    if manager == "apt":
        # sudo resets the environment, so pass DEBIAN_FRONTEND through env.
        return [as_root(["apt-get", "-q", "update"]),
                as_root(["env", "DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive", "apt-get", "install", "-y",
                         "--no-install-recommends", *missing])]
    return [as_root(["dnf", "install", "-y", *missing])]


def detect(args) -> int:
    info = read_os_release(args.os_release)
    print(f"{info.get('ID', '?')} {info.get('VERSION_ID', '?')}: {package_manager(info)}")
    return 0


def check(args) -> int:
    manager = package_manager(read_os_release(Path("/etc/os-release")))
    packages = read_packages(args.packages)
    missing = [p for p in packages if not is_installed(p, manager)]
    for p in packages:
        print(f"{p:<12}{'missing' if p in missing else 'installed'}")
    if missing:
        print(f"{len(missing)} of {len(packages)} package(s) missing")
        return 1
    print(f"all {len(packages)} packages installed")
    return 0


def apply(args) -> int:
    manager = package_manager(read_os_release(Path("/etc/os-release")))
    packages = read_packages(args.packages)
    # TODO 3: make the list of missing packages. If nothing is missing, print
    #         "Nothing to do: all N packages are installed" (N is how many there are) and return 0.
    missing = packages
    print(f"Missing {len(missing)} of {len(packages)} package(s): {' '.join(missing)}")
    for cmd in install_commands(missing, manager):
        if args.dry_run:
            print(f"would run: {shlex.join(cmd)}")
        else:
            subprocess.run(cmd, check=True, timeout=1800)
    if not args.dry_run:
        still = [p for p in missing if not is_installed(p, manager)]
        if still:
            print(f"error: still missing after install: {' '.join(still)}", file=sys.stderr)
            return 1
        print(f"Installed: {' '.join(missing)}")
    return 0


def main() -> int:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Install the packages a machine needs, only if missing.")
    sub = parser.add_subparsers(dest="command", required=True)
    p = sub.add_parser("detect", help="show the distribution and its package manager")
    p.add_argument("--os-release", type=Path, default=Path("/etc/os-release"), help="os-release file to read")
    p.set_defaults(func=detect)
    for name, func, text in [("check", check, "show which packages are installed"),
                             ("apply", apply, "install the missing packages")]:
        p = sub.add_parser(name, help=text)
        p.add_argument("packages", type=Path, help="file listing one package per line")
        p.set_defaults(func=func)
        if name == "apply":
            p.add_argument("--dry-run", action="store_true", help="show the commands without running them")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    try:
        return args.func(args)
    except FileNotFoundError as e:
        print(f"error: no such file: {e.filename}", file=sys.stderr)
        return 2
    except ValueError as e:
        print(f"error: {e}", file=sys.stderr)
        return 2
    except subprocess.CalledProcessError as e:
        print(f"error: {shlex.join(e.cmd)} failed with exit status {e.returncode}", file=sys.stderr)
        return 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

modules.summary: Bring Python and Linux together into automation you can leave running: wrappers around system commands, configuration from environment variables, logging an operator can rely on, and schedules with cron and systemd timers.

lessons.title: Wrapping Linux commands in Python
objectives: Wrap a command-line tool in a Python function with a clean interface
Get reliable data from commands by preferring machine-readable output
key_points: Wrap each command in a small function that builds the argument list, runs it with a timeout, checks the result and returns plain Python data, so the rest of the script never handles raw text or exit codes.

Prefer machine-readable output where a tool offers it: ip -json addr, lsblk --json, findmnt --json, df --output=pcent,target and systemctl show nginx --property=ActiveState --value are far easier to parse than the default tables.

Some commands answer with their exit status: systemctl is-active --quiet nginx exits 0 only if the unit is active, and grep -q exits 0 if anything matched, so a returncode == 0 test is the whole answer.

When there's no structured output, parse defensively: skip header lines, split with a maximum number of fields, and raise a clear error if the format isn't what you expect, rather than return wrong numbers.
Check that a command exists before relying on it: shutil.which("systemctl") is None in many containers and on WSL without systemd, so the script can say what's missing instead of crashing.

objectives: Read, validate and change environment variables from Python, including for child processes
Configure a tool from the environment, with sensible defaults and precedence
key_points: os.environ maps variable names to strings: os.environ["HOME"] raises KeyError when a variable is missing, while os.environ.get("LOG_LEVEL", "INFO") returns a default instead.
Changing os.environ affects the running script and any processes it starts afterwards, never the shell that started it: a child process can't change its parent's environment.

subprocess.run(cmd, env={**os.environ, "LC_ALL": "C"}) gives one child a modified copy of the environment; LC_ALL=C makes command output predictable, with no translated messages or local number formats.

Environment variables are always strings: convert and validate them, as in int(os.environ.get("MAX_AGE_DAYS", "7")), and stop with a clear message when one is invalid. A common precedence is command-line option, then environment variable, then config file, then default.

Keep secrets such as API tokens out of code and out of command-line arguments, which other users can see with ps; pass them in environment variables or in files with 600 permissions, and never write them to logs.

lessons.title: Logging for automation scripts
objectives: Replace print statements with the logging module, at the right levels
Configure where logs go: standard error, a rotating file or the systemd journal
key_points: logging gives each message a level, DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR or CRITICAL, and the configured level decides which are recorded; logging.getLogger(__name__) gives each module its own named logger.

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(name)s: %(message)s") is enough for most scripts. It writes to standard error, which cron can redirect to a file and systemd sends to the journal.

Pass values as arguments, as in log.info("archived %s", path), so they're formatted only if the message is recorded; inside an except block, log.exception("...") logs at ERROR level with the full traceback.
RotatingFileHandler(path, maxBytes=1_000_000, backupCount=3) caps a log file's size by rotating it; a service run by systemd can simply log to standard error and let the journal store and rotate it.
Log what an operator needs when something breaks at 3 a.m.: what started, what changed, what failed and why, with identifiers such as file names, but never passwords, tokens or personal data.

lessons.title: Scheduling with cron and systemd timers
objectives: Schedule a Python script with cron and with a systemd timer
Find out why a scheduled job that works by hand fails on schedule
key_points: A crontab line has five time fields, minute, hour, day of month, month and day of week, then the command: 30 2 * * * runs at 02:30 every day and */15 * * * * every 15 minutes. Edit with crontab -e and list with crontab -l.

cron runs jobs from your home directory with a minimal environment (PATH is often just /usr/bin:/bin), so use absolute paths to the script and to the virtual environment's python, and redirect the output, as in >> ~/job.log 2>&1.
In a crontab, % ends the command and starts its standard input, so write date +\%F; and flock -n /tmp/job.lock command skips a run while the previous one is still going.

A systemd timer pairs a .timer unit (OnCalendar=*:0/5 for every five minutes, Persistent=true to catch up on runs missed while the machine was off) with a .service unit of Type=oneshot that runs the script.

systemctl enable --now name.timer starts a timer; systemctl list-timers shows its last and next runs, systemctl status name.service the last result, journalctl -u name.service the output, and systemd-analyze calendar checks an OnCalendar expression.
A long-running Python program becomes a service with ExecStart= using absolute paths, User= a non-root account, Restart=on-failure, and Environment= or EnvironmentFile= for its settings.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Check disk space, memory, commands and services; log the results; exit 1 if anything is wrong.

Settings come from environment variables:
  HC_PATHS        mount points to check, separated by spaces (default: /)
  HC_DISK_WARN    the percentage used that counts as a problem, 1-100 (default: 90)
  HC_MEM_MIN_MB   the least available memory that's acceptable, in MB (default: 200)
  HC_COMMANDS     commands that must be installed, separated by spaces (default: python3)
  HC_UNITS        systemd units that must be active, separated by spaces (default: none)
  HC_LOG_FILE     also log to this file, rotated at 1 MB (default: standard error only)
  HC_LOG_LEVEL    DEBUG, INFO, WARNING or ERROR (default: INFO)
Exit status: 0 all checks passed, 1 a check failed, 2 a setting is invalid.
"""
import logging
import os
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys
from logging.handlers import RotatingFileHandler

log = logging.getLogger("healthcheck")


def setting_int(name: str, default: int, low: int, high: int) -> int:
    """A whole-number setting from the environment, checked against a range."""
    # TODO 1: read the variable called name from os.environ, using str(default) if it isn't set.
    #         Convert it with int(). If that fails, or the number isn't from low to high, raise
    #         ValueError(f"{name} must be a whole number from {low} to {high}, got {raw!r}")
    return default


def setup_logging() -> None:
    level = os.environ.get("HC_LOG_LEVEL", "INFO").upper()
    if level not in ("DEBUG", "INFO", "WARNING", "ERROR"):
        raise ValueError(f"HC_LOG_LEVEL must be DEBUG, INFO, WARNING or ERROR, got {level!r}")
    handlers: list[logging.Handler] = [logging.StreamHandler()]  # standard error
    # TODO 2: if HC_LOG_FILE is set, add a RotatingFileHandler for that file to handlers
    #         (maxBytes=1_000_000, backupCount=3). Then call logging.basicConfig with level=level,
    #         handlers=handlers and format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(name)s: %(message)s"


def check_disk(path: str, limit: int) -> bool:
    usage = shutil.disk_usage(path)
    percent = round(usage.used / usage.total * 100)
    ok = percent < limit
    log.log(logging.INFO if ok else logging.WARNING, "disk %s is %d%% full (limit %d%%)", path, percent, limit)
    return ok


def available_memory_mb() -> int:
    """MemAvailable from /proc/meminfo: what new programs can use without swapping."""
    with open("/proc/meminfo", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for line in f:
            if line.startswith("MemAvailable:"):
                return int(line.split()[1]) // 1024  # the file gives kB
    raise RuntimeError("MemAvailable not found in /proc/meminfo")


def check_memory(minimum: int) -> bool:
    available = available_memory_mb()
    ok = available >= minimum
    log.log(logging.INFO if ok else logging.WARNING, "memory: %d MB available (minimum %d MB)", available, minimum)
    return ok


def check_command(name: str) -> bool:
    path = shutil.which(name)
    if path:
        log.info("command %s found at %s", name, path)
    else:
        log.warning("command %s not found on PATH", name)
    return path is not None


def check_unit(unit: str) -> bool:
    """Ask systemd whether a unit is active: systemctl is-active exits 0 only when it is."""
    if shutil.which("systemctl") is None:
        log.warning("cannot check %s: systemctl not found", unit)
        return False
    # TODO 3: run  systemctl is-active UNIT  with subprocess.run (a list; capture text output;
    #         timeout=10). Log "unit %s: %s" with the unit and the first line it printed, at INFO
    #         if it exited with 0 and at WARNING otherwise, and return True only for exit status 0.
    return False


def main() -> int:
    try:
        setup_logging()
        limit = setting_int("HC_DISK_WARN", 90, 1, 100)
        min_mb = setting_int("HC_MEM_MIN_MB", 200, 0, 1_000_000)
    except ValueError as e:
        logging.basicConfig(format="%(levelname)s %(name)s: %(message)s")
        log.error("%s", e)
        return 2
    log.debug("settings: disk limit %d%%, memory minimum %d MB", limit, min_mb)

    results = [check_disk(p, limit) for p in os.environ.get("HC_PATHS", "/").split()]
    results.append(check_memory(min_mb))
    results += [check_command(c) for c in os.environ.get("HC_COMMANDS", "python3").split()]
    results += [check_unit(u) for u in os.environ.get("HC_UNITS", "").split()]

    failed = results.count(False)
    if failed:
        log.error("%d of %d checks failed", failed, len(results))
        return 1
    log.info("all %d checks passed", len(results))
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

[Unit]
Description=Server health check (disk, memory, commands, services)

[Service]
Type=oneshot
User=deploy
Environment=HC_DISK_WARN=85
Environment="HC_COMMANDS=python3 git"
ExecStart=/usr/bin/python3 /opt/healthcheck/healthcheck.py

[Unit]
Description=Run the server health check every 5 minutes

[Timer]
OnCalendar=*:0/5
Persistent=true

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target

If the service fails, journalctl -u healthcheck.service shows the traceback; a wrong User= name is a common cause.

project.title: devsetup: automate a developer machine with click
project.brief: Your team spends half a day setting up each new developer's Linux machine by following a wiki page. Replace the page with devsetup, a click command that reads a profile (profile.toml) and makes the machine match it: it installs the listed packages with apt-get, creates the directory structure under a base folder, and writes starter configuration files such as ~/.editorconfig. devsetup plan shows what would change without changing anything; devsetup apply makes the changes and is safe to run any number of times (a second run reports nothing to do, and an existing file that differs is replaced only with --force, keeping a .bak copy); devsetup check exits with 0 when the machine matches the profile and 1 when it doesn't. It detects the distribution from /etc/os-release and refuses one it doesn't support, logs what it does to the screen and to a file under ~/.local/state/devsetup/, uses exit statuses consistently, and installs as a command with pip or pipx. The starter files give you a profile, a pyproject.toml, a first plan command and three tests to build on. Prove it on a fresh Ubuntu 24.04 machine or container: plan, apply, apply again, check.
deliverables: The devsetup package: a pyproject.toml with a [project.scripts] entry, and code split into modules (for example cli.py, profile.py, packages.py and files.py)
A profile.toml for your team, with at least five packages, four directories and two files
At least eight pytest tests using CliRunner, tmp_path and monkeypatch, so no test installs anything or touches your real home folder
A README.md: what devsetup does, how to install and run it, its exit statuses, and how to run the tests
A transcript from a fresh Ubuntu 24.04 machine or container: plan, apply, apply again, check with its exit status, and the log file

# What a new developer machine needs. devsetup reads this file.

[packages]
apt = ["git", "curl", "jq", "tree", "python3-venv", "make"]

[directories]
base = "~/work"
create = ["projects", "scratch", "notes", "bin"]

[[files]]
path = "~/.editorconfig"
content = """
root = true

[*]
indent_style = space
indent_size = 4
end_of_line = lf
insert_final_newline = true
"""

[[files]]
path = "~/work/notes/README.md"
content = "# Notes\n\nWorking notes, one file per topic.\n"

[build-system]
requires = ["setuptools>=61"]
build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta"

[project]
name = "devsetup"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Set up a developer machine from a profile, safely and repeatably"
requires-python = ">=3.11"
dependencies = ["click>=8.2"]

[project.optional-dependencies]
test = ["pytest"]

[project.scripts]
devsetup = "devsetup.cli:cli"

[tool.setuptools]
packages = ["devsetup"]
"""devsetup: set up a developer machine from a profile, safely and repeatably."""

from click.testing import CliRunner

from devsetup.cli import cli

PROFILE = """
[packages]
apt = []

[directories]
base = "{base}"
create = ["projects", "notes"]
"""


def write_profile(tmp_path):
    path = tmp_path / "profile.toml"
    path.write_text(PROFILE.format(base=tmp_path / "work"), encoding="utf-8")
    return str(path)


def test_plan_lists_missing_directories(tmp_path):
    result = CliRunner().invoke(cli, ["--profile", write_profile(tmp_path), "plan"])
    assert result.exit_code == 0
    assert f"create directory {tmp_path / 'work' / 'projects'}" in result.output


def test_plan_skips_directories_that_exist(tmp_path):
    (tmp_path / "work" / "notes").mkdir(parents=True)
    result = CliRunner().invoke(cli, ["--profile", write_profile(tmp_path), "plan"])
    assert "notes" not in result.output


def test_a_missing_profile_is_reported(tmp_path):
    result = CliRunner().invoke(cli, ["--profile", str(tmp_path / "nope.toml"), "plan"])
    assert result.exit_code == 1
    assert "profile not found" in result.output
